#7740. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7739. ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7738. Former judge accused of shooting gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters

Former Oklahoma Judge Jerry Herberger was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters. (Photo from the Stephens County Sheriff’s Office)

A former Oklahoma judge was arrested recently after allegedly shooting a gun toward unwanted trick-or-treaters who came near his home on Halloween.

Former Judge Jerry Herberger, 73, of Duncan, Oklahoma, was booked in the Stephens County Jail in Oklahoma for assault and battery with a deadly weapon, attempted murder and possession of a firearm while intoxicated, the Lawton Constitution reports.

Police were called Saturday night after witnesses said an intoxicated Herberger had threatened trick-or-treaters if they came to his home. With a gun in his hand, he allegedly fired off a round in the children’s direction, according to the Lawton Constitution.

As officers prepared to make contact at the home, Herberger allegedly pointed a gun at one of the officers, said Loisdawn Jones, the director of communications for the city of Duncan, Oklahoma. He then complied with officers’ commands and exited the residence, where he was taken into custody and booked into the Stephens County Jail.

#7737. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7736. Crime and the city: Harbin, China

Harbin, capital of China’s Heilongjiang Province—what used to be known as Manchuria—China’s “Wild East.” It’s long been China’s most northerly and Russified city—train lines into Russia and for many decades run by the Russians to the warm-water port of Dalian and connecting to the Trans-Siberian Railway. And then, after 1917, a new Russian influx fleeing the Bolsheviks.

Even today, sitting up towards the border at the Amur River between China and Russia’s vast Far Eastern provinces, the city has onion dome Orthodox churches and synagogues with streets that would not look out of place Khabarovsk or Tomsk. But this is certainly Chinese territory now and so crime writing is, as we’ve seen in Crime and the City columns on Shanghai, Beijing and Chengdu subject to certain censorship and restrictions.

Yangsze Choo’s The Fox Wife (2024) is set up in Manchuria in 1908 where young woman is found frozen in the snow. Her death is clouded by rumors of fox spirits, believed to lure people into peril by transforming into beautiful women and men. Bao, a detective with a reputation for sniffing out the truth, is hired to uncover the dead woman’s identity. Since childhood, Bao has been intrigued by the fox gods, yet they’ve remained tantalizingly out of reach. Until, perhaps, now.

American Sinologist Scott Seligman’s true crime Murder in Manchuria (2023) is a brilliant evocation of the Soviet spies and fascists, adventurers and chancers who gathered in interwar Harbin, a city at once highly modern—trains, art deco hotels, American cars—yet with old world animosities that boil over into kidnapping, murder and espionage.

Semyon Kaspé, a young Jewish musician, is kidnapped, tortured, and ultimately murdered by disaffected, antisemitic White Russians, secretly acting on the orders of Japanese military overlords who covet his father’s wealth. When local authorities deliberately slow-walk the search for the kidnappers, a young French diplomat takes over and launches his own investigation. Amazing…. And it’s all true!

Novelist Mark Oulton fictionalizes this same period in Red Spy in Harbin 1: In the Making (2025). It’s 1935 Harbin, a city of spies, racketeers, and would-be revolutionaries. Chinese agent Chen Minghe is ordered to infiltrate the Russian émigré Fascist Party—led by Konstantin Rodzaevsky, a real-life White émigré whose vanity and erratic leadership belie his dangerous ambitions. 1937 dawns and full-scale war with Japan begins, Chen’s mission starts to unravel. Rodzaevsky’s affair with a planted mistress comes to light. The resulting scandal begins to unravel the operation.

Chen’s adventures in espionage continue in Red Spy in Harbin: Book 2: The Price of Survival (2026) but in this tale move to World War Two Japanese occupied Taiwan.

Another series with Harbin at its centre and in the same “nest of spies” interwar period is Tom Stickel’s Special District: Harbin: Drawing the Tiger’s Bones (2022). It’s 1929 A patrolman, Borya Melnikov, sits at the bottom ranks of Harbin’s Special District police force. A dismembered body. A raging Red Terror campaign. A brewing war with the Soviet Union….Borya is assigned to investigate the dismembered body of one the city’s foreign businessmen uncovered in the nearby Japanese zone.

Special District: Harbin: Book 2: The Tigers of East Mountain (2023) starts with the discovery of body of a local Jewish businessman in a Harbin back alley threatens to tip the city into mob violence… It’s 1932 and Borya Melnikov returns to police ranks after the Japanese take over Harbin and end Soviet control, only this time with the Judicial Police of the new state of Manchukuo (Japanese- occupied Manchuria).

And finally, Special District: Harbin: Book 3: Visiting the Tiger’s Den (2024). It’s 1935, and Borya Melnikov has risen to the rank of Senior Inspector on Harbin’s Judicial Police unit in Manchuria. But his position is becoming untenable as Manchukuo’s Japanese masters are increasingly intolerant of his independent style…and now this anonymous threat lands on his desk. It’s not in his nature to back down to threats, but it is only weeks before his wife returns to Harbin. He must quickly solve all four of his open investigations before she arrives or risk putting her into danger also.

Brian Klingborg’s City of Ice (2021) is more contemporary and has Harbin partially as a backdrop. In a remote Chinese town – where the theft of a few chickens counts as a major crime—a young woman is found brutally murdered…with her heart, lungs and liver removed.

Inspector Lu Fei, a weary cop who fled the city, suddenly finds himself under the intense scrutiny of the ruling party in Beijing. Determined to find her killer, Lu Fei must navigate a society where politics can be deadly, corruption is rife, and the powerful are untouchable. As evidence connects the case to a string of unsolved murders, Lu must decide what he will risk in search of justice….

There are more Lu Fei novels, mostly set in northern China, including Thief of Souls (2021), The Magistrate (2023) and Wild Prey (2022), which takes Lu Fei to Myanmar.

Caroline Petit has written several historical fictions set in China, usually southern China—Hong Kong and Macao. The Fat Man’s Daughter (2006) ranges too from Hong Kong up to Manchuria. In Hong Kong in 1937 orphan 19-year-old Leah Kolbe is approached by a Mr. Chang, who claims to have known her father and offers her a commission to go to Manchukuo to smuggle out Chinese Imperial treasures. She consents and, accompanied by her faithful amah and a Russian émigré woman in Chang’s pay, takes the train north.

And finally, a writer I’ve been trying to squeeze into Crime and the City for a long time, Japanese author Haruki Murakami. Not naturally a crime writer admittedly but his novel The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle (1994) counts I reckon. Toru Okada, an unemployed man living a quiet suburban life in Tokyo, watches his life unravel after his cat disappears, his wife Kumiko grows increasingly distant, and he starts receiving strange phone calls.

From there the story explores deep psychological trauma, historical violence (particularly Japan’s actions in World War Two in Manchuria), personal alienation, and the hidden depths of human memory. The Manchurian sections of the novel are extremely atmospheric and often harrowing, a stark, visceral departure from his usual dreamlike, whimsical magical realism.

It is a book partly about Japan’s war crimes in China, brutality and multi-generational trauma. A trauma, by the way, that still lingers over Heilongjiang Province and the city of Harbin.

Paul French is a British author of books about modern Chinese history and contemporary Chinese society including Midnight in Peking and the 2018 release City of Devils.

#7735. Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

“Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”

“This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

#7734. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7733. Kim Kardashian aims to retake bar exam

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian speaks onstage during the 2020 Winter TCA Tour on Jan. 18, 2020, in Pasadena, California. (Photo by David Livingston/Getty Images)

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian still holds ambitions to become a lawyer and plans to retake the bar exam—someday.

Kardashian, who failed the California bar exam in 2025, said she is “always thinking about the bar” and is “still all in,” she told People on Monday. “I’m going to take my time and wait until the moment is right, when I have some free time to focus on it.”

Kardashian, who plays a lawyer on Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair, was among the 7,362 candidates who completed the July 2025 administration of the California bar, according to the State Bar of California.

The state’s test is considered one of the most difficult in the country, and only 54.8% passed last year and 48.3% in July, according to the state bar.

Kardashian did not attend law school and does not have an undergraduate degree. She has followed the state’s alternative pathway that allows candidates to take the bar exam by learning the law through apprenticeship and study.

California is one of the few states that allow lawyers to become lawyers by “reading the law.”

#7732. A Guide to the Blofelds

There’s a lot of talk going around lately about the casting of the new James Bond. Who will play him… Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, CrimeReads favorite/dark horse Josh Bowman? This question is all well and good… but I want to know if this new leg of the franchise is going to have a Blofeld. Because, notoriously, the 007 films can’t keep it together around this guy.

Who is Blofeld? Ernst Stavro Blofeld, Bond’s archnemesis. He’s a megalomaniac who keeps trying to take over the world in one way or another. Oftentimes, his face is hidden. Sometimes, he’s in a wheelchair. Usually, he is petting a cat. One time, he’s Bond’s adopted brother, kind of.

The whole Blofeld situation is a bit nuts, with a total of nine different actors playing him (in various capacities), across the different chapters of the franchise.

A preamble: EON became embroiled in a legal dispute surrounding Thunderball that had serious implications for the different Blofelds. As noted in the book The Battle for Bond by Robert Sellers, Ian Fleming had based his novel Thunderball on a 1959 script for a film that he had written with his associates Jack Whittingham, Kevin McClory and Ernest Cuneo. Apparently, the story changed considerably and the writers went through multiple versions. In March of 1961, McClory, read an advance copy of the novel and contacted Whittingham, with whom he petitioned the courts to slap the novel with an injunction to stop it from being published. The judge who heard the case that month, permitted the novel to continue being published, though he didn’t ban any further legal action from taking place. Fleming suffered a heart attack during this time, but survived.

The suit (McClory and Whittingham v Fleming, Jonathan Cape Ltd and Bryce) went to court in November of 1963, and the case lasted three weeks. Fleming had two more heat attacks during this process. The men settled the case out of court, agreeing that Fleming was to retain the rights to the novel (as long as further editions credited the story as having been created by McClory and Whittingham as well as Fleming), while McClory and Whittingham won film rights. Fleming died of a fourth heart attack the following year.

What does any of this have to do with Blofeld? Walk with me.

First, multiple actors played the role as a continuous character in the Connery era: Anthony Dawson as Blofeld’s body and Eric Pohlmann as his voice in both From Russia with Love (1963) and Thunderball (1965), then Donald Pleasance in You Only Live Twice (1967). This change-up of actors poses no real issue to the films, because we don’t see his face at all in those first two films; the first time we get to see his face, it’s Pleasance. Continuous enough, fine.

Here’s where it gets wacky. Well, wackier. After You Only Live Twice, EON (the company that produces the Bond films) cast a new 007, George Lazenby, to begin a new era of the franchise. Telly Savalas plays Blofeld in that film, On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969). But then Lazenby quit, setting the Bond franchise adrift. They brought back Connery to play Bond in 1971’s Diamonds are Forever, and so cast a new Blofeld: Charles Gray.

This was Connery’s last EON Bond film, with the producers bringing on Roger Moore to start a new era with 1973’s Live and Let Die. But the battle between Kevin McClory and the Fleming estate continued; the original 1963-64 settlement gave way to more lawsuits over who owned what. During this time, EON was not allowed to use any of the elements from Thunderball, which seemed to include the character Blofeld and the organization SPECTRE.

EON had a thing or two to say about how little the Bond franchise needed Blofeld. In a bizarre pre-credits sequence in the 1981 Moore film For Your Eyes Only, Bond casually kills Blofeld by using a helicopter to lift him up and drop him (robotic wheelchair, cat, and all) into a smoke stack, before proceeding with its main narrative. That Blofeld also didn’t show his face; his body was played by John Hollis with voicework by Robert Rietty. He’s also not referred to specifically as Blofeld (for legal reasons, obviously). But the message was clear.

Later legal verdicts in the battle for the rights to Thunderball, especially a landmark one in 1983, confirmed that McClory in fact owned numerous elements of the Thunderball story, and therefore the Bond franchise, as well as that he could make his own movie adaptation of Bond elements as long as they were based on the Thunderball film. So he made his own film, Never Say Never Again, that year, casting Max von Sydow as Blofeld, and Sean Connery as Bond.

Blofeld remains absent for the final Moore film A View to a Kill (1985), both Timothy Dalton films, all four Pierce Brosnan films, and the first three Daniel Craig films.

McClory, who continued to sue for rights and royalties to the Bond properties for the rest of his life, died in 2006. His family resolved the issues with the Fleming estate and EON productions, selling the rights to EON’s parent company in 2007, paving the way for Blofeld’s eventual return in Spectre (2015). In that film, and in the final Craig film No Time to Die (2021), he is played by Christoph Waltz, marking the first time that a single actor has played Blofeld (in both body and voice) across two films.

#7730. U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A U.S. government contractor was arrested by the FBI this morning for allegedly leaking national defense information to another individual who repeatedly posted classified information to an online publication.

“National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The details alleged in this affidavit reflect the behavior of a government contractor who exempted himself from a federal law governing the protection of classified information. The Department of Justice will continue prosecuting individuals who leak classified information and put our national security at risk.”

“The FBI arrested the subject after he was caught allegedly betraying his oath and leaking classified defense information,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI - and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice.”

“Following a referral from the Agency, on Friday, October 23rd, the FBI arrested a contractor who provided services to CIA for alleged unauthorized disclosures of classified information,” said CIA Director John Ratcliffe. “The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers. There is absolutely zero tolerance for leaking, and anyone who violates their oath will be held accountable and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably. Those cleared to hold our Nation's secrets undertake a solemn obligation to protect that information. If proven at trial, this conduct is a grave violation of the Espionage Act, and the National Security Division will prosecute it as such.”

Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of the District of Columbia was arrested following a search of his residence and charged by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

According to the criminal complaint, beginning in 2020, the defendant worked as an employee of a U.S. government agency based in the Eastern District of Virginia and later in 2022 began working as a developer for systems integration for “Company 1,” a contractor to the same U.S. government agency. During all times relevant to the complaint, Brinksman held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the complaint, Brinksman had an ongoing personal relationship with an individual who maintains an online publication on Substack (Individual 1). A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 claimed Individual 1 had “published reporting based on classified [relevant U.S. government agency] assessments.” Individual 1 posted on her social media profile, “I also accept leaks.”

The FBI Chicago Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the Washington Field Office.

Trial Attorneys Eli Ross and Kathryn DeMarco of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Vito Iaia for the Eastern District of Virginia are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Stuart Allen for the District of Columbia.

Charges in a complaint are merely allegations, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7729. Apropos of nothing, you should watch The Night Agent

The “apropos of nothing” in this title is a joke, because (I’m writing this descriptively for posterity), America just experienced several historic wins in the 2026 midterm election, and therefore, made great headway in the fight against fascism. A blue wave, indeed.

I was thinking about something fun to recommend you watch as you come down from the incredible high of knowing our country is back in capable hands and we all might survive, and it hit me: The Night Agent. That’s an enjoyable show about political corruption and how good people can make it go away.

The Night Agent! It’s a spy thriller, not too gritty but still suspenseful. It’s the kind of thing you’d like if you wanted Air Force One to be a little less silly. The premise? There’s a guy (an FBI agent) whose job is to sit in the White House basement, manning a phone that never rings. Except one night, it rings. HOW GREAT IS THAT? I love it. (It’s based on the 2019 novel by Matthew Quirk.)

Our agent at the desk, Peter Sutherland (Gabriel Basso) immediately follows protocol… but winds up in over his head as he encounters a situation that poses a threat to honest American leaders, puppeteered by some not-so-honest ones. There are three seasons available on Netflix. Season four is coming out next year, so you should get ready.

#7728. Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled. (Photo by imaginima/Getty Images)

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.

#7726. Seeking Justice in Deep South Georgia

I had finished the third run-through of my closing argument, so I went down to the pond to see how John Petrey, my chief assistant district attorney, was doing with his portion.

I walked slowly and quietly so as not to disturb him. As I drew near, I caught sight of him standing on the dock, facing the water in his T-shirt, shorts, and Birkenstocks. Tall and slim, glasses perched on the end of his nose, hair a little disheveled, he was delivering a persuasive argument to what appeared to be an empty pond.

Across from the dock, though, I spotted the gray snout and black eyes of an alligator, the rest of the animal still and immersed in the water. The animal was watching him. Because the sun was shining from that direction, the light combined with Petrey’s terrible eyesight caused him not to see it.

That old gator was the most attentive juror he ever addressed.

We were two hundred miles from where the murder happened, living in a hunting lodge outside Albany, Georgia, preparing to close the biggest case I would ever try.

Eighteen months earlier, on December 15, 2000, during a cold and rainy night in Georgia, Derwin Brown, the sheriff-elect of DeKalb County (one of the largest metropolitan Atlanta counties), was ambushed and shot twelve times in his own driveway. The killing sent shockwaves through the Atlanta area and Georgia and was reported nationally and even internationally. The preceding summer, Brown defeated the incumbent sheriff in a highly contentious campaign that was focused on corruption allegations against the sitting sheriff. An investigative reporter for a local television station exposed shocking details of the corruption. Brown was three days from being sworn in. His family was inside the house waiting for him.

Derwin’s wife ordered a custom-tailored sheriff’s uniform for the swearing-in. She had hung it inside the storm door so it would be the first thing he saw when he entered the home.

At the morgue that night, I noticed his wedding ring had been flattened. A bullet had struck it. He had apparently been holding his hand up to defend himself.

As the district attorney, I had a policy that my team would show up any time an officer was killed in the line of duty, which is how I found myself alone with the bullet-ravaged body of Sheriff-elect Brown for a few minutes. I knew that if we found the killer(s), I would be the prosecutor.

The trial was not held in DeKalb County. There had been too much media coverage. The judge granted the defense request to move the trial.

The prosecution and the defense each got to suggest three cities. One of mine was Savannah. If I was going to spend eight weeks somewhere, I thought it would be nice to be near the ocean.

People who hear “change of venue” may think of it as a technicality, or as a strategy of defense attorneys to seek out a different jury pool. It should be neither. It occurs because a judge in the county where the crime occurred determines the people who live there are not impartial, and the case needs to be moved to another county to ensure justice is delivered.

When the order came in, I thought Petrey was playing a joke on me when he announced the case would be tried in Albany, the county seat of Dougherty County, in deep South Georgia. My hometown. I have three generations buried in that sandy soil below the gnat line in Georgia.

A few years before the trial, a hundred-year flood caused the Flint River to flood over the cemetery. The caskets were hermetically sealed, so when the flood water reached them they shot up out of the ground like missiles. Fred Mays, a GBI agent and one of the most important people on my prosecution team, once told me there were two things in this world he was afraid of: rattlesnakes and dead people. During that flood, Fred’s job was to take a motorboat out over the cemetery and lasso the caskets and bring them back.

My grandmother was buried in one of the caskets that floated down the Flint River. I always wondered if Fred was the one who returned her casket to the cemetery.

The trial was held in the county courthouse where I had been sworn in as a young lawyer, and where the state of Georgia once prosecuted Martin Luther King Jr. I watched Dr. King march down Slappey Drive when I was a boy. I stood on the sidewalk with Sarah, who cared for my sister and me, and I had no idea what I was looking at. I thought it was a parade.

Forty years later, I stood in that courtroom and quoted Dr. King to a jury.

The hunting lodge was the only place we could find in the Albany area to house our team of lawyers and investigators without interruption for two months. It had a cabin that looked like the one in the old Snuffy Smith cartoon. Seventeen miles outside town, it had a tin roof, a ladder up to a sleeping room with windows on every wall, and the pond. No phones. No television. Other small cabins were also on the grounds of the hunting lodge. This is what the biggest corruption and murder prosecution in the history of the state looked like from the inside. Lawyers in shorts, isolated from the outside world, arguing to the woods.

Months before, a lawyer who had worked in my office as an assistant district attorney came to my house.

He told me not to ask him any questions. He said he knew I did not carry a gun, but I needed to start carrying one, and I needed round-the-clock security.

Lawyers are allowed to break client confidentiality when a life is in danger. My name was on a hit list.

In Georgia, as in almost all states, the district attorney is elected and answers only to the people he or she serves. (This is in contrast to the federal system, where the United States Attorneys are under the supervision of the Attorney General who serves at the pleasure of the President.) It was my decision, and my decision alone, whether to bring charges against those whom I believed were responsible for Brown’s assassination. After sharing the evidence with the most experienced lawyers on my staff and seeking their input, Tom Clegg, my chief trial assistant, said, “You are the boss. It’s your decision.” Attorney General Robert Jackson, who was later appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court, said in a speech in 1940, “The prosecutor has more control over life, liberty, and reputation than any other person in America.”

A fair question is why I decided to be the lead prosecutor on this case. First, I was a career prosecutor who had tried over 100 jury trials before being elected district attorney. In many district attorney offices, especially in urban areas, the district attorney is primarily an administrator and rarely goes to court.  Some elected district attorneys have never tried a felony case, either as a prosecutor or defense attorney. The courtroom was my sandbox.

Second, the ultimate responsibility for a conviction or an acquittal would rest on my shoulders as the district attorney. I wanted to be in charge if I was to bear the responsibility for a win or a loss. Also, I had some of the best and most experienced trial lawyers in the country assisting me. I was not alone.

Finally, this case was critically important to the people I was elected to serve. A sheriff-elect was murdered before he could take the oath of office. The voters of one of the largest urban counties in the country had their vote taken away from them before the candidate of their choosing could serve. Our investigation revealed a pattern of corruption on a scale that none of us could have imagined before the murder.

As I put pen to paper to write the story of this case in A Rainy Night in Georgia (Prometheus/Simon & Schuster), I was struck by how the issues in this case remain relevant and timely today. The strength of our criminal justice system depends on having people who are committed to public service, integrity, and adherence to the rule of law.

Petrey gave his part of the closing argument to a jury of twelve. (It was a while before he learned about the juror with a snout.)

When the verdict came in, a reporter I had known for years, the one who had helped break this case in the first place, asked me what I was going to do next. I told him I was getting a six-pack, my Jimmy Buffett CDs, and my boom box, and I was going to the beach.

We chose Bermuda. My family appreciated being out of the public eye, on an island with some of the strictest firearms laws in the world.

J.Tom Morgan served as the elected District Attorney of DeKalb County, GA, from 1992-2004. He was the first recipient from the United States to be awarded the Special Achievement Award from the International Association of Prosecutors in 2003. Prior to his time as DA, Morgan served as an Assistant District Attorney in DeKalb County for nine years and was the first prosecutor in Georgia--and one of the first in the nation--to specialize in the prosecution of crimes against children. As a nationally recognized expert on criminal justice, he has appeared on The Oprah Winfrey Show, The Today Show, CNN, Court TV, and 48 Hours, among others. Morgan has lectured to prosecutors and law enforcement officials in more than 30 states, Puerto Rico, and Europe, and served on the faculty of the National College of District Attorneys.

#7725. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7723. Kennedy Cole on writing about race through invasion horror and parasitism

This essay will break down the themes of racism, homophobia, and existing as other that I touch on in There Used to Be People Here. I’ll expand on my thought process behind Samuel’s dilemma with the taur, and explore some of the complex moments that happen in the book (as much I can without spoilers). Imposter syndrome and belonging are two of Samuel’s biggest struggles; I plan to touch on that in aspects of my own life, and as an issue Black people deal with as a whole.

Foreign occupation of the body has always been a particularly terrifying horror element to me. The idea of losing control of not just our mind, but our being—autonomy, duality, and person—sounds so far out there that to some, it might be too impossible to fear.

Of course, it is an impossibility, in some ways. Very rarely, if ever, does one quite literally lose control of themselves to an outside source. In some ways, though, the idea is very real.

Take imposter syndrome, for example, the intrusive thought that you as an individual don’t belong in a room you’ve been—presumably—welcomed into. It happens to all of us, doesn’t it? We question our ability to be, wonder whether or not we truly belong in a space we, more often than not, do.

We allow, then, ourselves to change. We lose ourselves to paranoia. We become invisible in a space that originally valued us because of our unique ability to shine.

In my debut, There Used to Be People Here, Samuel Barkley is the only Black detective in a small police department in Mississippi, 1978. He works alone by choice, but also by default. He consistently questions his own worth, mostly as a result of the constant stares and pressured environment created by the officers around him, but also as a result of his own deeply buried trauma. Things shift when he’s introduced to a new case—a strange murder that starts in a gay bar—and an odd new partner who he has uncertain feelings about, Harvey Wilkins.

And of course Samuel wonders, do I deserve this?

As a Black woman, I’ve often asked this question myself whenever I find I’ve been given new, and most often exciting, opportunities. I attended a predominantly white K-12 school from Kindergarten until graduation, so trust me when I say I’ve had my fair share of stares and pressure and deeply buried trauma.

I’ve also had privilege: the privilege to learn at a private institution, to explore creative writing in a passionate environment, to research subjects I love and be encouraged to grow. At every turn, though, I found myself questioning my (what I now know is natural) ability to do so.

I found myself questioning my Blackness, because many other people around me—both Black and white—were doing the same. Was I truly talented, or was it a case of borrowed opportunity? Were my dreams tangible, or faraway wonders? Could I truly achieve all that I set my mind to, or was I just the only Black girl pretending to be white?

The taur—the worm-like, parasitic hive-mind antagonizing Wenton, Mississippi in my debut—propose this question in the most fitting way possible: by occupying the body. They feed on Samuel’s twisted desire to be invisible by creating an environment where this is true. To Samuel, the taur’s true motivations are murky, but their plans are clear: to make everyone, everywhere the same.

The idea of sameness can be beguiling to those of us who face discrimination because of our innate, unchangeable qualities. Samuel’s position as a detective in the Wenton Police Department is earned, and yet his role as the only Black man in the room pushes him to call his sense of self into question, much like I did as the only Black girl in my grade for thirteen years. It’s easy to wish ourselves away, to wonder whether homogeneity would erase the questions and stares altogether and allow our inner selves to shine.

And though in theory it would, our innate, unchangeable qualities are lost as a result. Our Blackness—which, even in a room full of people who are not, does matter—becomes invisible. We forfeit our bodies. We allow the parasite within us to win.

Throughout the story, Samuel’s autonomy does become forfeit, not because of a parasitic entity infecting him, but because of his own fear of existing as other. His queerness, which he discovers through his unique partnership with Harvey, is something he attempts to fold away for later. Over time, Samuel’s work as a detective shifts from a childhood dream to a tool determining his self worth. Working his way up through the ranks is his only true talent. And to Samuel, his Blackness is only an obstacle.

When I first began writing There Used to Be People Here, my identity had yet to be fully determined. In many ways, it still is wholly undiscovered. I’m a twenty-three year old woman publishing my very first book, preparing to be married to the love of my life in just under a year, and still looking for a job in my field long after graduating with a bachelor’s degree. I’m living this life for the first time, taking it one day at a time just like everyone else.

My sense of self, though, is much stronger than it was when I started my debut. I can think of no better reason for this than Samuel.

I parallel my novel’s main character in more ways than one. What frightens him frightens me. As Samuel works through his fear of unifomity—and the temptation to try it for himself—I was finding my voice as a queer Black writer.

To be blunt, writing about my race has been difficult for me. Up until this point, I’d never centered any of my stories around a Black main character, let alone a Black man. I wouldn’t realize it until I was well into drafting, but writing There Used to Be People Here challenged everything I’d learned about what it means to be a writer. My own work forced me to face the pattern I’d perpetuated, and in the context of the story, forced Samuel to look inward and face himself.

Now, I can look back and map Samuel’s journey alongside my own. Our Blackness—our innate, unchangeable worth—destines us to be othered. So, we shine not in spite of it, but because of it. We choose diversity, not because we welcome discrimination, but because our differences are a direct reflection of our autonomy. We reject the parasite and embrace each other, because our worth is determined by the depth of our love.

Kennedy Cole is a speculative author with a BFA in Creative Writing and a Certificate in Publishing. Born in North Carolina, she lives by the beach with her partner and enjoys playing games, puzzling, sipping matcha, and collecting tattoos. Her creative portfolio includes an array of published fiction, poetry, and nonfiction with Oakland Arts Review, Carolina Muse, Second Story Journal, and others. There Used to Be People Here is her first novel.

#7722. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
